lines.text: [indistinct audio - not transcribable]
Oh my God, Lord, please take my sunshine away. [singing] Don't hit him! The church called. The church called. [beat] Church? Yeah, they want their choir back. [everyone laughs]
You taking a picture? Yeah. Why's your phone so big? Hi, come here. Mama, do the "church called." What? Church. Church called. They want their choir back. Oh! [laughing]

[announcer voice] Hello, everybody. Welcome to the Island of Love and Trust, with your hosts David Choe, Critter Fleming, and a very, very special guest tonight. I mean, we say that all the time, but... But this is, like, the fans demand it.
They've demanded it. The moment is here. She's here. You've asked for it: Mrs. Jane Choe. [applause] Hi, baby. Hi, Mom. DVDASA, y'all! Give me a hug. Oh, great son, I love you. I love you too, Mom.

Super son. Oh, oh, oh, oh. Mom, give me a quick hug. Oh, yeah. Sorry — long time no see. Yeah, long time no see. So it's been... I've been on the island for one week now. Yeah. And, you know, it's a complete waste to have this giant mansion on the beach to myself once Critter and Harry left, so why not have my

parents come and enjoy a good time. So we've been running around doing a bunch of activities. You okay to be interviewed right now, Mom? Yes, sir. Just normal. Nothing to be scared about. You nervous? No. No screaming? Nothing? No. Okay.
Let's try to keep it — you know, the way me and my mom communicate is half Korean and half English, but my mom has lived in the United States for almost 40 years.

And so she can speak English. She chooses not to, because she... Well, I wanted you to be bilingual. Yeah, okay, whatever. So you're here. And one of the subjects we've been tackling — because I am here on this island where I did go to rehab.

And I'm on this island where it's a healing place. And, you know, when Harry was here with Critter, we did another show where I interviewed Harry. Oh, you did? And I didn't know that Harry's a giggle boy. Oh yeah, I love him. He laughs at everything — pain, misfortune, it doesn't matter. And so for someone like me,

who constantly chooses to focus on the negative, who whines and complains — I wanted to find out happiness. So one of the first things I want to tackle is the intro. As the sun was setting last night, I heard you and Dad singing. Yeah. So can you sing a song

to start us off into the show? I'm not a good [singer], but I can. Okay, thank you. What kind of song, same or different? Anything you want, Mom, it's up to you. I'm gonna try. Yeah, that's the song. I always love to do that.
Mom, sing your most favorite song that you like to sing. Okay, I'll do that. [singing] Watashi wa ureshii, watashi wa ureshii, watashi wa ureshii, itsumo ureshii...

Don't you remember, we usually sing this when you were little? So it's easy. That was fantastic. Yeah, we sing it together with his grandmother too. That was my mom singing "I Am Happy" in four different languages — Japanese, Chinese, English, and Korean.

You learned the Japanese from your grandmother? So, because the Japanese enslaved Korea when my parents were young during wartime, my grandmother and my two oldest aunts were not allowed to use their Korean names — they were forced to have Japanese names, and they spoke perfect Japanese.

I grew up with mostly Japanese friends — the Nambas, the Chigos. I didn't really have Korean friends. And Harry doesn't really count, because he looks like he's from Guam or Mongolia. [laughing] So you'd think people who were brutalized by the Japanese would be mean to my Japanese friends.
But they weren't. No, they weren't mean at all. I had Japanese people come to my house all the time. But like I'm saying, I got that song from your grandmother.

Yeah, she taught you in Japanese. She spoke Japanese very well. When my Japanese friends would come over, my grandmother would talk to them in Japanese, and she would not blame them for the sins of their fathers.
They were just kids, you know, there to have fun. However, they didn't like Joey, because he would come and eat all the seaweed. Grandma didn't like that. [laughing]

So let's start from the beginning. First — that was a beautiful intro and a great song selection: "I Am Happy." Thank you. [announcer voice] Welcome one, welcome all. This is DVDASA, from a secret location.

So, Mom, everywhere I go, I record shows. Oh, I didn't know that. Yeah, and you should never listen to them, and you should never know this exists. No, I didn't know. But you're here, and we just had a huge meal, and we're all a little bit up, so I figured, why not do this?

Oh, great. And everyone always asks about you — they love you. Oh, thank you, thank you everybody. On Anthony Bourdain: Parts Unknown, they love you. Whenever they see you at your art shows, or my art shows — oh, it was incredible. Thank you to all the people that came here.
All the fans that came to see you at your... I was so shocked. Yeah — my mom and Critter had their first art show. Let's hear it for them! [applause] Thank you, thank you everybody.
It was awesome. Last year — two years ago. It's my third one. With you. What do you mean? No, no, I'm talking about two years ago, or a year and a half ago.

Critter had never painted anything. You were begging Dad to paint art. Yeah, I asked him to buy the paint every single time we'd travel. My dad, to me, was a magician growing up — he could paint anything. He'd look at it and freehand it, and I was like, as a kid, that's literally the same

thing as magic. And then technology — a flat-screen TV in the '80s and '90s so they could watch Korean soap operas. Back then, to watch Korean dramas you had to go to the video store and get VHS tapes someone recorded in Korea and sent over. But now, with technology, Dad can watch Korean soap operas and Korean news 24/7, college basketball, women's golf.

So with my dad and my mom retiring, one of my greatest hopes was that my dad would start painting again — because this whole time it's been "I don't have time, I don't have time." I agree with you. Nothing but time now, right? And my mom and dad have both taken a huge active interest
in my life now that I'm an artist. So my mom knows everything about Leonardo da Vinci. Yeah, I read about it. Give us a fact about Andy Warhol that most people don't know.

Oh, I love Andy Warhol. He disciplined himself — he did 100 push-ups every day. Andy Warhol did 100 push-ups every day. And 200 pull-ups. For self-discipline. Yes, I like him. See, now I wake up every morning and it's on my list of things to do, and I never do it.
On my hand I write, "Today: 200 push-ups." You can start it. You have a plan. I really appreciate it — 10 things to do. A plan that I never follow. But it's okay, you keep praying.
And according to my mom, Andy Warhol's mother would give him a Hershey bar for every sketchbook page he finished. And also, he was gay. So they took an active interest in my life.
They're like, "Oh, our son's an artist, he makes a living in art." So my mom and dad are frequent guests at the museums and art galleries. Yes. They go on the LA art walks.
I mean, they're on the scene. They're on the LA art scene. And so... Do you know how many wigs Andy Warhol had? How many? Guess. I have no idea.

400. 400 wigs? Wow, I didn't know that. Yeah. This is what I mean — my mom has non-stop knowledge of all kinds of things. No, I just read a book, that's it. What about Leonardo da Vinci — any facts about Leonardo?

Oh, he only did 25 paintings. Only 25 paintings? Uh-huh. Is that true? Because he did a lot of different professions — he was an architect. So his art is mostly sketches. You mean actual finished paintings?
Who did the Mona Lisa? Leonardo da Vinci. Yeah, he only did 25. Oh, interesting. And there are only 10 left. I didn't even know that. See, I just read it not too long ago. And what about clothes?

What kind of clothes did he wear? He designed his own, right? He designed everything — a true artist. According to my mom, he was a genius, so he was an architect, he did everything, and that's why he focused on other things. But when he went outside, his clothes were perfect.

Oh yeah, perfect — no paint, no paint. You would never know he was an artist. Like, we go out and it's, "Hey, look at us, we're artists, there's paint all over our clothes." His were impeccable, not a drop of paint on them. Why don't you do that? It's really hard. I made a

conscious choice years ago to have painting clothes — these are clothes I only wear when I paint, so I don't have to ruin more t-shirts. I don't know why my voice just cracked. And I'd have my straight, clean, pressed clothes for

when I want to look nice. I mean, it's been a long time since I wanted to look nice, and it's impossible, because I end up painting everywhere I go and get messy. And I use my hands a lot, and when I paint I like to go crazy. That's you. It's okay, it's your style.

Everyone's had this experience of walking into a museum, seeing a painting, and going, "I could do that." So that's my dad. My mom goes with my dad, and my dad goes, "What is this? I could do this. I could do this." What do you say to Dad? "Do it. Just do it." He says, "Oh, I'll do it." He never says no. [laughing]

How many paintings does he owe you? How many has he promised you? Not only paintings — he owes me millions and millions of dollars, because way back, if we'd bought that one... Oh, he talks you out of buying paintings that end up being worth money.
Yeah, he says, "I'll paint it better than that." Oh, so not only does he owe you, he owes you a better painting. Right. We're about to buy it, and it's gone up in value.
Right, right. That's why I told him, "We gotta buy this one," and he said, "No, I can paint better than that, I'm not gonna buy that. That Rothko? I could paint that."

Quick question. Yes. Did you like my paintings? Would you have bought one of my paintings? Oh yeah. Do a serious critique of Critter's paintings, because your painting styles are much different. You're like me — fast and furious, very loose and sloppy.
You paint as much as you can and then you pick... I need more inventory. No, but you paint a lot and then you pick the good ones, instead of making just this one precious, you know.

You're right. And Critter — he puts a lot of time into it. He picks the right photo reference, then he sketches it out. A lot of preparation. Then he spends a lot of time mixing the paint, and then he does it.

It doesn't look like it, but he spends a lot of time. Oh, yes. I respect your preparation. How many paintings did you have? Seven. Critter had seven paintings — which, if he were Leonardo da Vinci, would be like half his life's work. And then my mom had more like a hundred paintings,

which was a selection out of thousands of paintings you've done in a year. So your style is more like mine. Yeah, I've got this piece of paper — around a thousand pieces. That's how many you've done this year? No, since 2011, the last two years, I don't know. So you just crank them out.

Oh, you've seen it. I mean, that's a small one. Yeah, it doesn't matter, you're just going for it. Yeah. Every single one is different. She paints on everything — that's drawing, this is painting, she paints on and draws on everything. She paints on the wall, she draws on

the wall, she puts everything up. We went to see Frozen on Thanksgiving and they gave us free popcorn buckets — she painted on that. She paints on rusty buzz saws, on bark that falls off our tree. I mean, she's an art monster.

But that's good. I've seen it, I love it. It's a self you're exploring and discovering. I love it. Good thing. That's all that matters. I just did it while we watched TV together with my husband — I'd sit next to him while he was watching, and I just did

a little bit. Yeah. This is what happened when we came home. So this is my dad's attitude: "I can paint better than this, don't spend your money on that. Oh, that's awful." And then reality sets in — he's not going to. Recently — I'm not supposed to make bets, but I made a

bet with Dad. Because all he cares about is that I get married and have children. And I said, if you paint three huge paintings and 20 small paintings — I gave him the homework this year — then I will seriously consider marrying one of these women I hang out with.
So that's a bet we made, and it's almost May now, and he's painted... You see, he's prepared. I'm going to bet him on Thursday for the basketball game.
Oh, you did? No, I'm going to. For a painting. So here's what happened. My mom complains to me. She goes, "He keeps telling me..." He has a huge house.
He can turn any of the extra bedrooms into a painting studio. I set it up. I bought him canvases, I bought him paint supplies, I bought him everything he could possibly use.
There's no way [he can't]. Why don't we go over and take the TV away from him? I think he would die if we did that. Just leave him alone. What would happen if we took the TV away?
He's a white boy — that I know. So my mom complains to me. She's like, "He keeps saying he's going to do it, but he doesn't do it." And so I say, "Why don't you do it?
You're creative. Your whole life is art. Everything you do is art — your fashion, the way you present yourself." I like it, yeah. And who cares if it's not perfect? And she went for it.

So when everyone announced the show — "Dave's mom and Critter, the bodyguard, art show" — people looked at it as a joke. But it's like, no, I really was proud of you guys. You did a great job, you took it seriously. And

it just goes to show, in this day and age, whatever the fear is that cripples you from creating something — you just do it. I love to do that. I like your colors. He was very stressed out at that time. Oh yeah. That's draining. It was a lot of

pressure for him. Hard to make the color. But his color is so deep — he wouldn't help me, so I had to get a color wheel. And then finally, once I started, he came down one day — I think he saw Roadie down there — and he was telling me, "Mix this color,"

and then I think Dave saw, and Dave came down about 20 minutes later, like, "Do you need any help?" Well, I actively went out of my way not to help you guys. Because everyone says on my birthday or Christmas, "Oh, it's so hard to shop for you,

what should I get you?" And there's nothing. That's why I started art. I told my parents a long time ago — first of all, they're the worst shoppers, they never get me anything I want. Since I was a kid. Now I sound like a brat, but they never get me anything I want.
Since I was a kid, I'm like, "I want this back scratcher," and then they'll buy me socks. They never get me what I want — they always get me what they think I want.

Sorry. And as a boy who's grown up to be a beautiful man now, who has everything he could ever imagine — I've bought every house, car, anything material I can have. It's impossible to shop for me. Anything I want, I order immediately, or have Bobby order it.

So I said to them years ago: the only thing I could ever want from you on my birthday or Christmas, if you ever want to give me a gift, is art. That's it. A song you're singing me, writing something, music, art — anything. So now they paint me cards all the

time. My dad draws me cards all the time, and it's the best present. There's nothing they could buy me that would be better than the art. But my mom is so attached to the originals, she only gives me color copies. I don't get why. Because you're moving around so much,

I don't know where you are, so I don't want you to lose my original. But here's the thing — the number one thing I hear from people who aren't artists — I don't even like telling people I'm an artist — is, "I'm not any good." And that's why I didn't want to help you guys with anything, because

I want to see — in the same way, when David Chang was on our show, he said he likes hiring kids who are raw, who didn't have any school but just have the passion and desire, as opposed to someone who went to school. I want to see what you guys make without proper art training, or

without me giving you tips. I want to see what comes out of you — whether they call it naive or folk art or whatever. Did you see my Christmas card? I love it. Was it a monkey? Yeah, I mean, my mom, you know. This one for his birthday. This year? Yeah, nice. He didn't see this one? No, he doesn't show me anything. That was for my birthday. Did he get the original? Yeah. Oh, you gave me the original? Yeah, because he's steady now. Oh, because it's my birthday. I mean, he was in New York, so I didn't want him to lose my original pieces.
One night, while Critter was working on his paintings, he says to me, "Dave, I have a real tough time painting noses." Look at you — you can't even get off your phone either. [laughing]

No, no, no, I want to show you. It shows later, okay. He says, "I can't paint the nose, it's too hard." Right. It's difficult. If you've never taken an art class and don't know how to bend the form or use light sources, it's sort of hard to do.
So I said, don't even paint the nose. Who cares? Just two dots. Or nothing. Who cares? It's art. You can express yourself any way you want. So Critter started the no-nose movement.

That's good. Now his paintings have no noses — that's his thing. Greatest advice I've ever gotten: if it's too hard, just don't do it. I mess up sometimes, and I just live like that. It's okay. It's art. There are no accidents.

So let's go back to the very beginning of this journey to Hawaii. Okay. How did you get to the airport? By airplane. No — to the airport. Who took you to the airport? Bill. Bill Poon. Bill Poon. Yeah. Now, how did...

Did you call Bill Poon, or...? No, somebody... Don't tell me you know Bill Poon. Yeah. How do you know Bill Poon? I don't know him — as he showed up, I thought he was a taxi driver. Oh, you thought a taxi was gonna take you, and Bill Poon shows up, and he says, "Oh, we know your son." Then what happened?

So Bobby called Bill Poon. Bobby sent me the email: "Mrs. Choe, the taxi will be there at 6:30 in the morning." He told you a taxi, and then Poon showed up. No — the transporter came and picked up. I thought the taxi arranged it. Okay. I hope he had a

sheet on the back seat. Did you guys sit in the back of the car, or the front? Front. Yeah, it's a small car. He asked me how many bags I have. I said just the regular two. So — I've been in a car with my mom from the Atlanta Herbalife

Extravaganza, and in the 15-minute distance from the airport to our hotel, I've seen her insult our cab driver — a fat guy — and sell him a weight-loss product within that 15 minutes. So what did you guys talk about in the car ride? Did he ask you questions? No, because

your dad sat in front, okay, I sat in the back. Because I'm not a morning person, and it was 6:30 in the morning, so, like anybody else. Dad's a morning person, he wakes up at five. So Daddy talked with him. Oh, so they talked. Okay, so I'll have to do another

separate interview — I would love to know what you and Bill talked about. But then you asked me last night if he's a chef. I know, I need somebody to help me cook a couple times a week. Did you think he was David Chang? No, did he say something about

cooking? Yes. Oh, Bill did? No, I didn't talk to him yet, because I'm asking you first. He talked about how he cooks. You know him. No, I know him, that's why I'm asking you. Maybe he can help me. Wait, you like Bill enough that you'd want him to come cook for you? If he can do it, why not? He cooks Chinese style, I don't mind. I'm looking for somebody who can help a couple nights, with the cleaning. I will definitely, definitely ask Bill when we get back. I'll even text you — your daddy needs it, because when he goes to the hospital...

Bill — if you like getting along with him. Yeah. My dad, sometimes when he doesn't feel like driving, just takes the bus, because he likes it. My husband — he never cooks. He's retired. My mom won't let him retire fully, because my parents take

separate vacations — sometimes my mom will go to Korea by herself with a friend, and then my dad, he just doesn't know how to take care of himself. He'll just eat out, or make ramen, Subway, ramen, McDonald's. Yeah. And hide candy everywhere. He's cute. So everyone knows in my family that I love Hawaii.

I come here all the time. Anytime I need to heal or need some quiet time, I come here. There are magic people here, there are future people here, and there's kimchi at almost every single restaurant, Korean or not. So — this is how Korean my mom is. Right after they get off the plane, we pick them up and take them to the poke shack,

where we get octopus, we get sashimi... Yeah, good, good seafood. And I thought they'd be pumped, because there's cucumber kimchi, normal kimchi, octopus kimchi. And my mom's like, "No, no, don't get it." I'm like, what?

She's like, "I got my own kimchi." I'm like, what do you mean you've got your own kimchi? Did you carry her suitcase out of the car? Yeah, it was so heavy. Not only did she bring her own kimchi from home, she brought her own rice. I'm like, okay, we'll bring this home,
because your father — yeah, my dad's diabetic. Well, I'm diabetic too now. No you're not. Hold the line. No, I'm not borderline anymore, I have it. No, you don't have to have it.
You're telling me, "God, take it away." Okay, I don't have it. If you have diabetes, you're not even supposed to eat brown rice. Well, it's better than white rice.
So my mom's like, "Don't get that." I'm like, "Mom, they have kimchi right there, let's get some to eat with this fish." And she's like, "I got my own." You get home, and half her bag is black rice.

I've never even seen black rice. Just a tiny amount. Little black rice — forbidden rice, I guess. And she just has her own kimchi. Do you understand how bad your bag would have smelled if that broke? No, I packed it very well, anyway. In sardines. What was that hot sauce, that red sauce? What's it called?

It's gochujang. It's the Korean hot sauce, it's amazing, you eat it with everything. Last time they came, they said they didn't bring anything, but you know they shop, but they don't have the right things, so maybe we'd need something. So I just brought

this time. So this trip right now wasn't even supposed to happen for my parents. It was supposed to be — what was it — Machu Picchu. Machu Picchu, your dad. I sat down with my dad on Thanksgiving and Christmas — his oldest sister, my aunt, passed away when she was 69, and he's about to be 69. I know he

likes to sometimes focus on all his friends dying and stuff. So I figured there's a bucket list of things he wants to do, so I asked him what his dream was. And through Herbalife — my mom and dad were Herbalife distributors for, what, the last

20 years. Champions, right? They got to the President's Team, they were friends with Mark Hughes. So they've gotten to see a lot of the world. Oh yeah. We actually came to Kona because of them 20 years ago, when I was like 17 years old. So my dad said
Peru — Machu Picchu. He wants to go to... you know what, I'm not even gonna say it, because I don't want to jinx it. But Peru was one.
And he's getting older, he's falling down a lot, he's forgetting a lot of stuff. So the Machu Picchu hike is pretty tough, right? I don't think it's the right time. It's not the right time.

So I said, watch it — donkeys. Well, yeah. And not only that, it's the oxygen. The altitude. So I said, I haven't seen him in a while. You know, when you have diabetes and you get bruised or hurt, it takes forever to heal.

So I said, one of my favorite hikes in the entire world is on the Big Island in Kona — Pololu Valley. That's perfect. I've had vision quests there, I've had dreams there, I've had visions. So I said I'll just take him there, and if he can do that... He had a tough

time yesterday. See, I told you. I know. And my dad — he's mastered the art of, I talked about this last time, when he wants to exit, he sings "So Long, Farewell" from Sound of Music. But now, when my dad is done, like right now, he'd be sitting here, but he's out. He

had one beer with Critter. Critter had 20 [bucks] on the Warriors, and my dad had 20 on the Clippers, and he lost, and the Warriors lost. And my dad was insulting — he had one beer, got drunk, got faded, and was insulting Critter the whole time. And then

as soon as the game was over, it was time to go to dinner. We just had an amazing dinner. I'm jealous. I was about to eat, and then Dave came down and goes, "You need to come upstairs." But my dad — dinner passed, and he just passed out.
He needs to eat. So — Bill Poon drives my parents to the airport, they get here, we go buy raw fish, no kimchi because my mom brought her own, and my dad's pumped.
Sees the house — it's right on the water. And we go, "Let's go, let's do activities." Now, my parents have limited energy reserves, so it's one activity a day. One for my dad.
Maybe two for you. Right, you're right. So my dad's like, "We're in Hawaii, I'm pumped, let's go!" Boom, he passes out. He's done, right? So Dad's pumped and then he goes right to sleep.
Four hours, straight out. Four hours, he's jet-lagged. So me, Critter, and my mom — we're right by the beach — go snorkeling, just the three of us.
Oh, I love that. It's fabulous. Yeah. And that's my dad's style — when he's done, he's done. There's no... But he's old, he's done his time, he's earned it. He's earned it.
We had dinner the other night, and we're in Hawaii. First of all, anyone who listens to the show knows I'm a very, very impatient person, running at the speed of a big city.
I'm not slow, I don't take things easy. You're right. So when you sit down at a restaurant in Hawaii, sometimes it takes 15 minutes before they even give you a menu. You don't get mad.

They're just — sometimes it's just one kid working there. Right. So we eat dinner and it just took too long for the check to come. My dad doesn't say "excuse me" or anything — he's just gone, he's up, and we're in the middle of a scintillating conversation, and he just disappears. That's his style.

So we get here, my dad's out, and the three of us — me, Critter, and my mom — go right down to the bay to go snorkeling. And I'm very calm, very relaxed. It was very relaxing, but scary for me, because you just dyed your hair, did you know that? So my mom is dyeing her hair red, and

when she came out of the water it's like — oh, I thought she was bleeding. She comes out of the water like that movie Carrie — red dye just dripping down her face. And I didn't even realize it. Mom, it was so scary. I didn't realize that.

So how many times have you been to Hawaii, Mom? Many. You've been here more than six, seven times? Yes. So my mom's not new to Hawaii. She's been snorkeling. And the thing everyone says non-stop when you go snorkeling in Hawaii: don't take stuff from the island, just leave it here.
Observe everything, just don't touch anything. Okay. Don't touch the fish, don't touch the coral, don't touch the turtles. I mean, my mom is making a scene at the beach. It's amazing.
It took you a while to learn the snorkel. Yes. And then you're shocking me with all the red hair dye. But then we get in the water, and we see a fish like this.

It's like a needle fish. Right. And you see it and you almost choke because you were laughing. You can hear her underwater — underwater, I hear her start laughing like someone just told the funniest joke, literally laughing at how stupid this fish looks. [laughing]

She goes up for air, still laughing, and she's like, "Did you see that fish?" I go, "Yes, I saw it too, but I don't laugh at it like this." And now everyone on the beach is like, "What is going on over there?"
And my mom is just dying, literally dying, from the sight of a fish. And I'm like — I've never seen that. But if I see something I've never seen before, I go, "Oh, I've never seen that before."
I go up like this because it's way high, so I can see it. And then she waves — she's always waving at the fish. Yeah. So I've swum with turtles before.

And I know, because I've been to Hawaii a lot of times — don't touch the turtles. Definitely, definitely don't touch the turtles. And the turtles, they know you're there. I've swum this close to a turtle, where I see them, and they know you're close.
Once, the turtle was swimming with his fins out, and I was like, oh, cool, I want to touch his fin to make it look like we're holding hands. He was like this — [pulling away].

Oh yeah? The turtle definitely, definitely isn't into you. The turtle definitely doesn't want to touch you. 20 feet — 20 feet, they say. And Critter, with his sight-beyond-sight eagle-eye vision — Critter's amazing.

He sees the halibut hidden, camouflaged. He sees all the fish that are hiding — I don't even see any of this stuff. And he sees the first turtle we saw, and he goes, pointing, "Hey, look, there's a turtle." So my mom, without even — it's a shallow reef — she
goes right over the coral, stepping on all the coral, and just picks it up. I know you're excited, but you can't control yourself. Oh, sorry. Was the turtle talking to you?

Yeah. I see the eyes. The eyes are so big. When I cross that turtle, he's gonna see me. I say yes. Wait, so even though you know it's not okay to touch the turtles, the turtles said yes with their eyes?

Yeah, I say hi, hi, and — oh my God. So that sounds familiar. Yeah, so the turtle said yes with her eyes, and that made it okay to touch? Wait, so what about the eyes? They're just big, and it's like, "Hold me, touch me"? No, I like it — the eyes, he's looking at me. So it's a real...
